extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, policymakers, and students interested in administrative law and executive policymaking
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly analysis of how presidential authority and institutional design interact with agencies' administrative capacity to produce (or impede) administrative policymaking. The piece examines mechanisms of control, sources of insulation, and tradeoffs between politicization and capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity as a necessary condition for presidential power
rubrics_metrics.description: For the President to exercise true control over administrative policymaking, they must have both agenda-setting authority and the power to direct the agency’s capacity toward that agenda; presidential control is necessary but insufficient — capacity is the other necessary condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit formulation from the text: "For the President to exercise true control over administrative policymaking, they must have both agenda-setting authority and the power to direct the agency’s capacity toward that agenda." The Article emphasizes treating capacity as an evaluative dimension of whether presidential preferences translate into policy outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoff between increasing presidential control and preserving capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reforms aimed at increasing presidential control are double-edged: strong adherence to unitary executive theory and politicization can weaken administrative capacity by reducing career employees’ autonomy and policy discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual guidance: "Reforms aimed at increasing presidential control are double-edged... strong adherence to unitary executive theory may have the unintended effect of weakening presidential power by reducing the administrative state’s capacity for policymaking." Examples: independent commissions often have higher capacity because they are insulated from politics; loss of autonomy reduces expertise investment and increases exit incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active management (not just spending) builds capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Building capacity does not always require increased spending; it requires promotion of active management and better managerial behavior from Presidents and appointees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article argues Presidents "have the greatest opportunity to improve administration but do not always behave as good-faith managers." It recommends vigorous management as an evaluative lever to improve agency capacity; courts, Congress, and the public should play roles in holding Presidents accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and components of administrative policymaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative policymaking comprises development of policy via rulemaking, executive orders, executive memoranda, guidance documents, and related devices; activities include collecting evidence, identifying alternatives, drafting regulatory text, soliciting and responding to public comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article gives both a broad and a narrower definitional note: broadly the development of policy using listed devices; narrowly "policymaking" as the activity of deciding on new policies. It lists concrete process steps (collecting evidence, identifying alternatives, drafting, responding to comments) that serve as criteria for assessing policymaking activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between agenda-setting and technical participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting among policy alternatives is agenda setting; an actor may participate technically in the policymaking process (e.g., drafting) without setting the agenda or deciding on new policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance stresses terminological precision: to avoid confusion, the Article distinguishes "agenda setting" from "policymaking" (deciding on new policies) and notes that participation in technical tasks does not equal agenda control. This distinction is an evaluative axis when judging who truly controls policy direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergent preferences between Presidents and career employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Presidents and career staff often have different policy preferences because they are selected differently and have different motivations (electoral/co-partisan goals vs. career-driven public service and agency missions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article identifies selection mechanisms (election vs. merit recruitment), ideological self-selection into agencies, and differing incentives (reelection/legacy vs. career-expertise) as causes. It uses agency examples (EPA, DHS) and literature citations to show this is a persistent, measurable phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency mission, culture, and esprit de corps shape policy outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection into like-minded agencies facilitates development of distinct missions, cultures, and policy preferences that orient agencies toward particular tasks and priorities (e.g., DOJ's enforcement culture; IRS's revenue-maximizing orientation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article treats organizational culture and mission as evaluative criteria for predicting agency responses to presidential direction and for understanding why agencies prioritize some tasks over others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for control mechanisms when preferences diverge
rubrics_metrics.description: When Presidents and agencies have divergent preferences, Presidents require institutional mechanisms to direct agency capacity toward their agendas; otherwise capacity can frustrate presidential priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This entry follows the theoretical argument: similarity between President and agency reduces need for coercive control; divergence increases need for mechanisms such as politicization, centralization, or other levers described elsewhere in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politicization of agency leadership as a control strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Presidents increase control by politicizing agency leadership—appointing loyalists, exempting positions from civil-service protections, creating personnel structures (e.g., the Senior Executive Service) to give Presidents greater influence over staffing and agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article cites the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 creating the Senior Executive Service and notes appointees' roles in setting agendas and spurring policy change. It also notes empirical/interview evidence that career employees generally accept politically appointed officials' authority when clearly exercised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization of policymaking within the White House (budget and agenda levers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Centralization—via budget control (Budget and Accounting Act/OMB), agenda coordination (EO 12,866 meetings, White House sign-offs), and restrictions on rulemaking volume—functions as a presidential control mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific mechanisms described: OMB's budgetary levers and apportionment, EO 12,866 annual priority meetings, Executive Orders requiring senior-appointee approvals, and OMB limits on number of concurrent rulemakings. These are concrete institutional criteria for assessing presidential control capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA regulatory review as a tool to align rules with presidential priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA reviews "significant" rules, prioritizes review of rulemakings related to presidential priorities, and substantively edits proposed rules to ensure alignment with those priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article describes OIRA's role and cites EO authorities; it distinguishes routine review from White House involvement in larger proposals and notes OIRA's editorial influence as an evaluative dimension of control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural independence (civil-service protections and independent commissions) as insulation from control
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil-service statutes, removal protections, fixed terms, and statutory constraints (e.g., party-balancing requirements) create insulation that limits Presidents’ ability to replace or direct agency policymakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article highlights 5 C.F.R. protections, statutory limits on commissions, and the greater insulation of independent agencies. These features are criteria for assessing how much presidential control can be exercised in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Career employees’ informational and procedural advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Career bureaucrats have superior information about substance and procedure, which gives them advantage over presidents' appointees and Congress; they can exploit procedural choices to shape policy outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support in text: career employees understand how proposed policies translate into outcomes and have expertise about procedural consequences; citations and quotes (e.g., Potter) indicate bureaucrats can capitalize on procedural complexity for political advantage—an evaluative factor in explaining policy persistence or resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: External political pressures (Congress, interest groups) influencing agency policymaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress and interest groups apply their own levers—agency design, budgeting, investigations, the Congressional Review Act, appropriation riders, comment submissions, and lobbying—to influence or constrain agency rulemaking and thus affect presidential control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article lists concrete statutory and procedural tools (CRA, riders, formal comments) and describes how these external pressures interact with agency capacity and presidential mechanisms. Use these factors when evaluating the feasibility of presidentially driven policymaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical link: capacity affects rulemaking completion and responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical results (discussed elsewhere in the Article) demonstrate that higher agency capacity correlates with greater completion of rulemakings and affects responsiveness to presidential agendas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article signals empirical findings (see references to Part III.B) showing capacity's measurable effect on rulemaking output; capacity therefore serves as an operational metric for comparing agencies' responsiveness to presidential direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms and examples of bureaucratic resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Resistance by career employees can take concrete forms—refusal to defend policies, removal of documents, use of dissent channels, or other acts—that impede presidential directives in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives examples: Acting AG Sally Yates refusing to defend travel ban, removal of NAFTA-withdrawal letter from the President's desk, State Dept. dissent cable signatures. These exemplars illustrate the kinds of behavior that count as resistance when evaluating the strength of presidential control.
